ComprehensionText:
Have you ever heard someone sing, "Happy birthday to you . . . happy birthday to you . . ."? If so, you are hardly alone—millions of people sing that song every year, and the tune is one of the most familiar of any song in North America.

Ironically, it is not known who wrote it! The tune was written by two sisters, Patty and Mildred Hill, who were school teachers in the late 19th century. But their song had different words; instead of "happy birthday to you," the song ran "good morning to all." The two sisters would sing this ditty to their students each morning as school began. In 1924, the tune was published in a song book, which added the "happy birthday" lyrics as verse two. Today, the second verse of that song has become one of the best known tunes in the world—and nobody knows who wrote the words!
QuestionText: Why is it ironic that the author of the words to "Happy Birthday" is not known?
AnswerA: because almost everyone knows the song
AnswerB: because it shows how unjust life can be
AnswerC: because of modern copyright laws
AnswerD: because it was published in 1924

How Animals Use Tools Tools are usually thought of as human inventions. But did you know that animals use tools to solve problems, too?

The chimpanzee, for example, uses grass stems to catch termites. This animal knows where these insects live. It pokes a stem into the termites' nest. Then it waits. Sometimes the chimpanzee has trouble locating water. When this happens, it often uses leaves as a tool. The chimpanzee pushes leaves into places that it cannot reach. The leaves soak up the water from these places. Then the chimpanzee chews on the leaves. Chimps have also been known to use sticks as digging tools.

The woodpecker finch is another animal that uses tools. It uses small sticks to pick insects out of tree bark. Another animal that uses tools is the sea otter. It uses rocks to crack open shellfish. Here is how. The otter places the rock on its chest. Then it holds the shellfish in its paws and bangs it against the rock. This cracks the shell open and allows the otter to eat the creature inside.

The green heron uses bait to catch fish, just as humans use bait on the end of a fishing pole. The heron does this by picking up a small object with its beak. Some animals have uses for tools other than gathering food and water. Some use leaves to dab at wounds or to clean. Some even use twigs as toothpicks. A scientist named Benjamin Beck discovered that crows are very good at solving problems. One unusual crow that lived in Beck's lab ate dry food moistened with a little water. When people forgot to add water to the food, the bird used a cup and added its own water. The elephant is one of the most intelligent animals. Using its trunk as an arm, the elephant puts grass and branches together. It then uses this tool to swat flies. When needed, this tool can also be used as a back scratcher. ComprehensionText:
We'd only lived in the street for a week when my mother sent me down to the corner shop on an errand. I'd already heard the horror stories about the shopkeeper. The kids from school called him Groucho.

That day, for the first time, I stepped from the bright warmth of the street into the musty, arctic gloom of the corner shop.

'What do you want, boy?' It wasn't so much a voice as the rumbling from a bottomless volcano.

A sharp thrill of panic spread through my body and in a rush, all the schoolyard stories came back to me. Two boys that Groucho had caught stealing a bar of chocolate now felt very ill whenever they saw or smelled chocolate. Without being seen, Groucho could sneak up on you like a vampire, floating silently from the other end of the shop. He'd just appear at your shoulder and ask what you were doing.

'My mother' was all I could manage to choke out.

I saw the ranks of milk inside the door of the tall fridge and with hands that felt like feet, I fumbled a bottle onto the counter and began tugging coins from my pocket. As my sweaty fingers grappled with the stubborn silver, I made the mistake of looking up.

Groucho was not so much clothed as swathed in odd rags and small blankets against the cold. They were grubby and stringy at the edges and looked as if he slept in them. He wore a strange old purple woollen cap that exactly matched the colour of his gigantic lumpy nose. The lines in his face were as deep as cracks in the pavement and his teeth jutted out at all angles like the stubs of yellow crayons. Although his eyes were a deep black, as he leaned down to stare at me, tiny glints of light danced and revolved like distant galaxies. The old hands that rested in front of him were the grimy claws of some prehistoric bird of prey.

I tried to place my money on the counter but I was already moving for the door. The coins jangled in the silence and I heard one make a butting roll and clang on the floor. I hit the door hard, forgetting it opened inward, then tore it back and burst into the sunshine clutching the milk against my pounding chest as I finally remembered to breathe.
QuestionText: How did the narrator feel when the shopkeeper spoke to him?
AnswerA: terrified
AnswerB: guilty
AnswerC: irritated
AnswerD: disappointed

The Wind's Handwriting
Grandad and I walked onto the beach early, before anyone else had left a footprint. The tide was out, and the wet sand stretched almost to the rocks.
'Look down,' said Grandad.
I looked. The whole beach was covered in ripples, long wavy lines lying side by side like the ridges on a tin roof. They went on and on, as neat as if someone had raked them.
'Who made these?' I asked.
'The sea did,' said Grandad. 'When water flows back and forth over sand, it rolls the grains along and piles them into ridges. The ripples line up across the way the water was moving.'
I crouched and ran my finger along one. Then I noticed something strange. Some of the dunes higher up had ripples too, even though the waves never reached that far.
Grandad smiled. 'What else moves sand?'
I thought about it. My hair was whipping across my face, and grains of sand were stinging my legs. 'The wind!' I said.
'Exactly. Wind and water both do it. Ripples are even found in old rocks that were once sand at the bottom of a sea.'
I took a photo of the dune ripples and another of the beach ripples. At home I put them side by side. They looked almost the same, as if the sea and the wind had been copying each other's handwriting.
By the afternoon, the tide had come back in, and the beach ripples were gone.

AnswerA: tidy
AnswerB: dirty
AnswerC: deep
AnswerD: tiny

ComprehensionText:
Gran's Fifty-Year Postcard
Gran had kept the postcard on her fridge for fifty years. It showed a penguin standing on an iceberg, and on the back, in faded pencil, she had written: One day.
Now, wrapped in a borrowed red jacket, Lily stood beside Gran on the deck of the ship as it slid into a bay in Antarctica. The water was as still as glass. Icebergs drifted past like enormous white sculptures, some streaked with a blue so bright it seemed to glow.
'Look!' Lily pointed. On the shore, hundreds of Adélie penguins waddled and squabbled, their black backs shining.
Small rubber boats carried the passengers to the beach, because the ship was too big to go near the shore. The air was so cold that it stung Lily's nose, and the snow squeaked under her boots. A penguin hopped right past her, carrying a pebble in its beak.
'They build their nests from stones,' said the guide. 'Sometimes they steal them from their neighbours.'
Lily laughed and turned to tell Gran, but Gran wasn't laughing. She was standing quite still, her gloved hands pressed to her mouth, and her eyes were shining.
'Are you all right?' Lily asked.
Gran nodded but didn't speak for a long moment. Then she pulled the old postcard from her pocket and held it up beside the real penguins.
'Not one day any more,' she said softly. 'Today.'

AnswerA: swam quickly

AnswerD: argued noisily

ComprehensionText:
Every Kid Needs a Pen Pal
Imagine opening your letterbox and finding an envelope covered in colourful stamps from a country you have never visited. Inside is a letter written just for you. I believe every primary school student should have a pen pal, and here is why.
First, a pen pal teaches you about the world. My pen pal, Hana, lives in a small town in Japan. From her letters I have learnt that her class cleans the school every afternoon and that she eats rice for breakfast. No textbook ever told me things like that.
Second, writing letters makes you a better writer. When you know a real person will read your words, you take more care with spelling and handwriting. My teacher says my writing has improved more this year than ever before.
Third, a pen pal teaches patience. A letter can take two weeks to arrive, and then you must wait again for a reply. In a world where messages fly back and forth in seconds, learning to wait is a useful skill.
Some people say pen pals are old-fashioned and that video calls are faster. That may be true, but a video call disappears when it ends. A letter can be kept in a shoebox and read again years later. I keep all of Hana's letters, and I have reread the first one so many times that the folds have gone soft.
So grab a pen and some paper. Your new best friend could be waiting on the other side of the world.

AnswerA: belonging to an earlier time
AnswerB: costing a lot of money
AnswerC: hard to understand
AnswerD: made by hand
